issue: The currency unit is wrong. Reparations were set at 132 billion gold marks (not pounds sterling). 132 billion gold marks was equivalent to approximately £6.6 billion or $33 billion USD at 1921 values. Stating '£132 billion' overstates the figure by a factor of roughly 20 and confuses the currency. GCSE students could lose marks quoting this.
correction: Reparations were set at 132 billion gold marks in May 1921 (the London Schedule of Payments). This was equivalent to approximately £6.6 billion pounds or $33 billion USD at the time.

lesson_title: Rise and consolidation of Nazi power, 1933-1934
claim: The purge — known as the Night of the Long Knives — killed approximately 85 to 200 people
issue: The lower bound of '85' refers to the announced/Gestapo list figure; the upper bound of '200' is one estimate. However, most modern historical scholarship gives higher estimates: Britannica and Wikipedia note that unofficial estimates put the death toll well above 200, with some estimates reaching several hundred. The lesson's '85 to 200' range, while not entirely wrong, understates the scholarly consensus range which commonly extends to 400+. As a secondary concern, the lesson elsewhere says 'Approximately 5,000 people were arrested' in the July Plot context (different lesson) — this is addressed separately.
correction: Casualty estimates for the Night of the Long Knives range from a minimum of 85 (the announced Gestapo figure) to estimates of several hundred; the precise total remains disputed. '85 to 200' is defensible but on the conservative end.

lesson_title: Life during the Second World War
claim: Approximately 5,000 people were arrested in the subsequent purge; around 200 were executed, including Stauffenberg.
issue: The arrests figure is significantly understated. USHMM, Britannica, Wikipedia, and multiple other authoritative sources state that approximately 7,000 people were arrested following the July Plot. The ~5,000 figure is closer to the number executed (approximately 4,980 executed), not the number arrested. The lesson conflates these two figures: it says 5,000 arrested and 200 executed, when in fact ~7,000 were arrested and ~4,980 were executed. The '200 executed' figure only captures the inner circle of direct conspirators, not the full reprisal purge.
correction: Approximately 7,000 people were arrested in the aftermath of the July Plot. Of these, an estimated 4,980 were executed — not around 200. The '200' figure represents only the most prominent direct conspirators. The full reprisal purge was far larger.

lesson_title: West Germany: economic recovery and politics
claim: By 1973 approximately 2.6 million Turks were living in West Germany
issue: The 2.6 million figure for Turkish residents applies to approximately the mid-2000s, not 1973. Between 1961 and 1973 around 867,000 Turkish guest workers travelled to Germany, of which around 500,000 returned, leaving roughly 600,000-900,000 Turkish nationals in West Germany by the time recruitment ended in 1973. The 2.6 million figure is around three times too high for 1973 and could seriously mislead students. The 2.6 million total Gastarbeiter (all nationalities) by 1973 is more plausible but conflates all nationalities with Turks specifically.
correction: By 1973 approximately 600,000-900,000 Turkish nationals were living in West Germany (not 2.6 million). The Turkish population reached around 2.4-2.6 million only by the mid-2000s. The total Gastarbeiter from all countries combined peaked at around 2.6 million by 1973, which may be the source of confusion.

lesson_title: The Berlin Wall and Cold War relations
claim: Kennedy visited West Berlin and addressed a crowd of approximately 450,000 people at the Rudolph-Wilde-Platz
issue: The 450,000 figure refers to estimates of people lining the streets of West Berlin during Kennedy's entire visit, not specifically to the crowd at Rudolph-Wilde-Platz (Rathaus Schöneberg). The crowd at Rudolph-Wilde-Platz where Kennedy delivered the 'Ich bin ein Berliner' speech is most commonly cited at around 120,000. Attributing 450,000 specifically to the square is misleading.
correction: Approximately 120,000 people gathered at Rudolph-Wilde-Platz (Rathaus Schöneberg) for Kennedy's speech on 26 June 1963. The 450,000 figure (or higher estimates of 1.1 million) refers to total crowds lining the streets of West Berlin during his entire visit, not the specific plaza audience.

claim: Between 1949 and 1961 approximately three million East Germans left
issue: Most authoritative sources give a higher figure of approximately 3.5 million (Berlin Wall Foundation, Britannica) to 3.8 million East Germans who emigrated between 1949 and 1961. 'Approximately three million' understates the commonly cited figure by half a million to nearly a million, which matters for students asked to provide precise statistics.
correction: Between 1949 and 1961 approximately 3.5 million East Germans emigrated to the West (some sources give up to 3.8 million). 'Approximately three million' is an underestimate.

claim: Between 1949 and 1961 approximately three million East Germans had emigrated to the West
issue: Same issue as Germany L5: the figure should be approximately 3.5 million (consensus of authoritative sources), not three million. This second instance of the same understatement reinforces the need for correction.
correction: Approximately 3.5 million East Germans emigrated to the West between 1949 and 1961. Multiple authoritative sources (Berlin Wall Foundation, Britannica, Wikipedia) consistently give this higher figure.

lesson_title: Life during the Second World War
claim: The firebombing of Hamburg in July–August 1943 (Operation Gomorrah) killed an estimated 37,000 people
issue: Casualty estimates for Operation Gomorrah vary significantly across authoritative sources: the most commonly cited range is 34,000–40,000 (Hamburg city archives, World History Encyclopedia), with some sources giving figures up to 46,000 or higher. The lesson's '37,000' figure is defensible but is stated definitively when historians note it is contested. More importantly, it is on the lower end and slightly below the most widely cited figure of approximately 40,000. Presenting a precise figure without noting the uncertainty is slightly misleading.
correction: Casualty estimates for Operation Gomorrah (July–August 1943) range from approximately 34,000 to 46,000 killed, with most sources citing figures around 37,000–40,000. The exact number cannot be determined with certainty.

claim: at the airlift's peak, one plane landed every 90 seconds
issue: The peak frequency of Berlin Airlift landings was one plane every 45 seconds (at Tempelhof airport during the 'Easter Parade' of April 1949), not every 90 seconds. Multiple sources including the Smithsonian National Air and Space Museum and other authorities cite 45 seconds as the peak interval. The 90-second figure may reflect an average during normal operations rather than the peak.
correction: At the peak of the Berlin Airlift (Easter 1949), one aircraft landed at Tempelhof every 45 seconds. The 90-second figure appears to be an average rather than the peak.

lesson_title: The Great Depression and the New Deal
claim: When around 20,000 First World War veterans marched on Washington in the summer of 1932
issue: The most authoritative and commonly cited figure for the Bonus Army is 43,000 total demonstrators (including 17,000 veterans plus families and affiliated groups), per Britannica and NPS. The National Parks Service and VA sources give 17,000 veterans specifically. '20,000 veterans' falls between these figures but does not match the most authoritative sources. The National Archives and Britannica consistently cite 17,000 veterans or 43,000 total. This is a minor point but could cause students to quote an inaccurate number.
correction: The Bonus Army comprised approximately 43,000 total demonstrators, including around 17,000 World War One veterans plus their families and affiliated groups. Citing '20,000 veterans' is an approximation that does not match the most authoritative figures.
